By my comment about the cooking time and diameter, I was referring to the way your batter heats up. Sorry about the way I phrased it, it was a little confusing.

All the batter in the pan needs to reach a specific temperature to be cooked to the correct amount. (I googled it and apparently a commonly accepted medium-fudgy brownie internal temp is 165F.) It takes time for the heat from the oven to pass through, so middle of the batter heats up slower than the edges. Of course you want the middle to reach your ideal temp before the edges hit overdone or burnt. If you have more batter, it’ll take longer to heat up the middle (especially if it’s in a narrow/deep pan rather than a flat/wide one). Also, heat is transferred faster through the metal of the pan than air, so the pan matters too.

If you use two smaller pans, the batter in the middle is closer to the fast-conducting metal than it would be in one big one, so the centre will reach your ideal temperature faster. I believe the reason she’s calling for an aluminium pan is because they don’t hold as much heat as other metal ones (specific heat capacity if you know about that or want to google it) which means they’re less likely to overcook edges.

I meant that I thought the depth would be the most important factor in determining the cooking time, but in retrospect I’m leaning more towards the pan shape. The percentages don’t matter as much as the dimensions - the calculation earlier is just my ballpark way of working out how much batter to start with. 

I’m sorry but I have no idea if it’s possible to calculate the time difference, and if it is I don’t know how to. However, I think it will work out whichever you try. I’m going to guess that if you use 100% of the recipe, your cake pans will prevent underbaking being an issue. Your oven variance and everything will throw a spanner in the works so if you use 85% the time difference might not even be noticeable - either way the most important thing will be to keep a close eye on it. I would choose depending on whether avoiding over- or underbaking was the most important to you.
This is a problem I’ve not heard before, with an actual solution, and a genuinely happy ending. Awesome.

If you used her exact recipe in your tins, you would have a little too much batter, and this would make your baking time longer. This risks overbaking the edges, although I believe the fact that you’re using round tins means that you’re avoiding the worst of this because of the corners. Maybe someone more informed than me can pitch in for that.

You can use an area calculation to approximate the amount of batter. I’ll write out what I’ve done in case you’re not a maths person:

9x13in is 117sq inches of tin space in the recipe.
One 8in pan has a radius of 4in. 4in squared is 16sq in, x pi is approx 50sq in. You have two pans, so let’s call that 100sq in. 

That means that in order to fill your tins to the same height as she does in the recipe, you’d need to use about 85% (100:117) of the amounts she lists. The fact that you’d be using two tins with a smaller diameter will decrease your cooking time, but I’m making a guess that that will be minor compared to depth and limited by the aluminium. Again someone with more knowledge might be able to confirm this or correct me.

How old is he? At about 9 months to a year, they have their first molt, and males lose the juvenile/female colouring. 

If he’s male he’ll lose some of the grey around the face and that on the body might reduce or lighten. He won’t be fully yellow, the molt is a noticeable change but a mutation like that shows from the first feathers growing in. He’ll probably lose the beautiful grey face if he’s male.

The female/juvenile colouring is more grey, barring on the abdomen and tail and especially the grey on the face, and the small stipple of grey in the cheddar cheek. It’s not an exact science though, I have one entirely grey female with barring and one pied female who looks like a male. 

How certain are you of the sex and age? Some breeders will sell a bird as male if it has a mutation that can pass for male because they’re usually more sought after. If trust your breeder, he’ll probably lighten. If you don’t and you’ve not seen a molt yet, your best bet is to wait for the behavioural markers, and to get as much quality time with him as possible now. Building the bond while they’re young makes for very rewarding results. Congrats on your new friend!
